description: The Aurelians is a team of AI enthusiasts, developers, and problem-solvers passionate about space and innovation. For the Flame in Freefall challenge, we aim to use AI, data analysis, and creative thinking to extract insights from microgravity combustion data and improve fire safety in space exploration. We welcome collaborative teammates skilled in AI/ML, software development, data science, design, and research.
summary:
Aurelius: Microgravity Fire Intelligence helps turn decades of NASA combustion research into evidence people can find, compare, and understand. Developed for the Flame in Freefall challenge, our interactive web dashboard addresses a critical information gap: valuable findings are scattered across publications and experimental records, making it difficult to connect research with questions about fire safety in space.

The platform combines a searchable research explorer, experimental comparisons, data visualizations, and an AI (Artificial Intelligence) assistant. Users can explore studies, inspect documented measurements, and ask questions in everyday language. The assistant retrieves relevant research and links its answers to supporting sources, allowing users to examine the evidence behind each response. Experimental conditions, missing values, and limitations remain visible to support careful interpretation.

Aurelius serves aerospace engineers, combustion researchers, professors, and students investigating fire prevention, detection, and suppression. As human exploration extends toward longer missions and future lunar and Martian habitats, making existing research accessible becomes increasingly valuable. Our contribution is a practical research tool that connects discovery, comparison, and explanation in one place, helping users build understanding while preserving scientific context and traceability.
details:
Flame Intelligence is an interactive research platform that makes NASA’s microgravity combustion research easier to discover, understand, and apply. It helps researchers, students, and mission planners explore how flames behave in reduced gravity, examine experimental conditions, and identify evidence gaps relevant to future space missions.

The platform brings together 20 investigation records, 40 source records, and a searchable archive of 12 NASA Technical Reports Server publications containing 720 indexed passages. Users can explore investigations, search publications, compare studies, inspect numerical evidence, and ask scientific questions. The research assistant retrieves relevant publication statements and connects them to their original sources, including publication titles, PDF page numbers, and supporting passages. This makes findings traceable and independently checkable.

A mission workspace lets users configure parameters such as oxygen concentration, pressure, and gravity context, then rank investigations by their research relevance. Comparison checks flag incompatible experimental conditions or evidence types. Downloadable reports preserve source references, ranking inputs, and reproducibility checksums, helping users document and communicate their research process.

The intended benefit is a more efficient and transparent path from a scientific question to supporting evidence. Bringing literature discovery, comparison, and source inspection into one workspace can reduce the effort involved in navigating technical reports. Its intended impact includes supporting research prioritization, engineering discussions, and science education while making specialist space research more approachable.

The project’s creativity lies in combining an evidence archive, a source-linked research assistant, transparent mission relevance rankings, and reproducible reporting within one accessible interface. Scientific uncertainty is part of the experience: missing measurements, gravity mismatches, and evidence gaps remain visible. Experimental observations and published model results are clearly distinguished, helping users interpret findings responsibly.

The frontend uses TypeScript, React, Next.js, Tailwind CSS, and GSAP. The backend uses Python and FastAPI, with SQLite FTS5 for text retrieval, PyMuPDF for publication text extraction, and Pydantic for structured data validation. GitHub supports version control and automated checks, while Vercel hosts the frontend and backend. The platform runs through a web browser and does not require specialist laboratory hardware.

Development prioritized scientific accuracy, source attribution, responsible data handling, reproducibility, mobile usability, keyboard accessibility, and support for reduced motion. Reliability was verified through 64 backend tests, 42 browser tests, and live deployment checks covering search, evidence retrieval, mission rankings, analytics, and report downloads.
